title: September 2021 Class College Final Supplementary Exam (Part 1 of 6)
unit: Comprehensive Nursing (Fundamentals, Anatomy and Physiology, Immunology, Parasitology, Psychology, Pharmacology)

sets.title: Set 1: Original Exam Questions
sets.description: The original MCQs from the September 2021 class College Final Supplementary Exam paper (Kenya Registered Nursing, sat 30 May 2024, Multiple Choice Questions, Q1 to Q20).

questions.text: A theorist who emphasized the caring aspects of nursing is:
questions.explanation: Jean Watson (C) is correct because her Theory of Human Caring (Philosophy and Science of Caring) places caring at the centre of nursing, using ten carative factors (later caritas processes) such as humanistic-altruistic values, faith-hope, sensitivity to self and others, and a helping-trusting relationship. Virginia Henderson (A) is incorrect because she defined nursing as assisting the individual with 14 basic needs until the person can do so independently. Dorothea Orem (B) is incorrect because her Self-Care Deficit theory focuses on the person's ability to perform self-care and when nursing is needed. Florence Nightingale (D) is incorrect because her Environmental theory focuses on manipulating the environment (ventilation, light, cleanliness, quiet, warmth, diet) to promote healing.

questions.text: Assault is:

options.A: The duty not to inflict harm as well as prevent harm
options.B: Threat to harm another with the ability to actually harm
options.C: Anything the person is touching or holding without consent
options.D: To render care based on education, experience, and circumstance

questions.explanation: Threat to harm another with the ability to actually harm (B) is correct because assault is an intentional threat or attempt to touch another person in a harmful or offensive way, which puts the person in fear of imminent harm, and the person making the threat has the apparent ability to carry it out (for example threatening to give an injection to a patient who refuses). Battery is the actual unconsented touching. The duty not to inflict harm as well as prevent harm (A) is incorrect because it describes the ethical principle of non-maleficence (beneficence is the duty to do good). Anything the person is touching or holding without consent (C) is incorrect because that describes battery, the unlawful physical contact (this includes anything attached to or held by the person). To render care based on education, experience, and circumstance (D) is incorrect because it describes the standard of care expected of a reasonable nurse, which is tested in negligence cases.

questions.text: On assessment, the nurse notes that the skin is intact but reddened on the patient’s heel. The nurse interprets this as:
questions.explanation: Stage 1 pressure ulcer (A) is correct because stage 1 is intact skin with non-blanchable erythema (redness that does not fade when pressed) over a bony prominence such as the heel, sacrum or trochanter, and it may also feel warmer, firmer or tender. Stage 2 (B) is incorrect because there is partial-thickness skin loss with a shallow open ulcer or blister, with a red-pink wound bed and no slough. Stage 3 (C) is incorrect because there is full-thickness skin loss with visible subcutaneous fat, but no exposed bone, tendon or muscle. Stage 4 (D) is incorrect because there is full-thickness tissue loss with exposed bone, tendon or muscle. Nursing care of a stage 1 ulcer is to relieve pressure (repositioning every 2 hours, heel offloading), keep the skin clean and dry, and avoid massaging the reddened area.

questions.text: The nursing positions for a patient who has difficult with breathing are:
questions.explanation: Standard Fowler’s, Orthopneic (B) is correct because both positions keep the trunk upright, so that the diaphragm drops and the abdominal organs do not press on it, giving maximum lung expansion. Standard Fowler's is a head elevation of 45 to 60 degrees, and the orthopneic position has the patient sitting up and leaning forward over an overbed table with the arms supported, which is used in severe dyspnoea, for example in asthma, COPD and heart failure. Low Fowler's and Sim's (A) is incorrect because Sim's is a semi-prone position used for rectal examination, enemas and for unconscious patients to drain secretions. Semi Fowler's and lateral recumbent (C) is incorrect because the lateral recumbent position is a side-lying position that gives no extra lung expansion, even though semi-Fowler's (30 to 45 degrees) can help breathing. High Fowler's and horizontal recumbent (D) is incorrect because horizontal recumbent (supine and flat) lets the abdominal contents push on the diaphragm and worsens breathing, even though high Fowler's (60 to 90 degrees) is helpful.

questions.text: Light palpation is used to asses:
questions.explanation: Tenderness (A) is correct because light palpation (pressing the skin about 1 cm with the fingertips, using gentle circular or dipping movements) is used to detect surface tenderness, muscle guarding, masses near the surface, skin texture, temperature, moisture and pulsations. Body organs (B) is incorrect because assessing the size and position of organs requires deep palpation (4 to 5 cm, often with a bimanual technique). Skin color (C) is incorrect because it is assessed by inspection. Bowel sound (D) is incorrect because bowel sounds are assessed by auscultation (and in the abdomen, auscultation is done before palpation and percussion so that the bowel activity is not altered).

questions.text: The most effective means to prevent transmission of pathogens is:
questions.explanation: Hand hygiene (A) is correct because the hands of health workers are the commonest route by which pathogens are carried from patient to patient, so hand washing with soap and water or rubbing with an alcohol-based hand rub at the WHO five moments (before touching a patient, before a clean or aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient and after touching the patient's surroundings) is the single most effective infection prevention measure. Personal protective equipment (B), inoculation injuries prevention (C) and equipment decontamination (D) are incorrect because, although each is an important part of standard precautions, they are supportive measures and do not have the same overall effect as hand hygiene.

questions.text: Cardiac muscles are:
questions.explanation: Striated and involuntary (B) is correct because cardiac muscle has cross-striations (organised sarcomeres), one or two central nuclei and branching fibres joined end to end by intercalated discs, and it contracts automatically under the control of the autonomic nervous system and the hormones, without conscious control. Striated and voluntary (A) is incorrect because it describes skeletal muscle. Non-striated and voluntary (C) is incorrect because no muscle has this combination. Non-striated and involuntary (D) is incorrect because it describes smooth muscle, which is found in the walls of hollow organs and blood vessels.

questions.text: Parasympathetic stimulation of the heart results in:

options.B: Decreased heart rate and decreased contractility
options.C: Decreased heart rate and increased contractility
options.D: Increased heart rate and decreased contractility

questions.explanation: Decreased heart rate and decreased contractility (B) is correct because the vagus nerve (parasympathetic) releases acetylcholine at the SA and AV nodes, which slows the rate of firing (negative chronotropic effect), slows conduction through the AV node (negative dromotropic effect) and reduces the force of contraction (negative inotropic effect, mainly of the atria). Increased heart rate and increased contractility (A) is incorrect because this is the effect of sympathetic stimulation (noradrenaline acting on beta-1 receptors). Decreased rate and increased contractility (C) and increased rate and decreased contractility (D) are incorrect because the autonomic nervous system changes rate and contractility in the same direction. Note: the effect of vagal stimulation on ventricular contractility is small, because the vagus supplies the atria much more than the ventricles, but of the options given B is the intended answer.

questions.text: The medial rectus muscle rotates the eyeball:
questions.explanation: Inwards (A) is correct because the medial rectus lies on the nasal side of the eyeball and turns the eye towards the nose (adduction); it is supplied by the oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III). Upwards (B) is incorrect because the superior rectus (with the inferior oblique) elevates the eye. Outwards (C) is incorrect because the lateral rectus abducts the eye and is supplied by the abducens nerve (VI). Downward (D) is incorrect because the inferior rectus (with the superior oblique, supplied by the trochlear nerve IV) depresses the eye.

questions.text: Calcitonin:

options.B: Inhibits reabsorption of calcium by renal tubules
options.C: Acts on the bones to increase blood calcium levels
options.D: Release is stimulated by decreased ionized calcium in the blood

questions.explanation: Inhibits reabsorption of calcium by renal tubules (B) is correct because calcitonin lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclast activity in bone and by reducing the renal tubular reabsorption of calcium (and phosphate), so more calcium is excreted in the urine. Is secreted by the parathyroid gland (A) is incorrect because calcitonin is secreted by the parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid gland, while the parathyroid glands secrete parathyroid hormone. Acts on the bones to increase blood calcium levels (C) is incorrect because that is the action of parathyroid hormone; calcitonin inhibits bone resorption and so lowers the blood calcium. Release is stimulated by decreased ionized calcium in the blood (D) is incorrect because calcitonin release is stimulated by a raised blood calcium (hypercalcaemia), and low calcium stimulates parathyroid hormone release.

questions.text: An example of external innate immunity is:
questions.explanation: Skin (D) is correct because the external (first line) innate defences are the physical and chemical barriers that keep pathogens from entering the body: intact skin and mucous membranes, sebum and the acidic skin pH, mucus and cilia, lysozyme in tears and saliva, gastric acid, and the normal flora. Inflammation (A), fever (B) and the complement system (C) are incorrect because they are internal (second line) innate defences, which act once the pathogens have entered the tissues, together with phagocytes, natural killer cells and antimicrobial proteins such as interferons.

questions.text: Mast cells are released during:
questions.explanation: Inflammation (C) is correct because mast cells in the connective tissue release (degranulate) histamine, heparin and other chemical mediators when the tissue is injured or an allergen binds IgE on their surface; histamine causes vasodilation and increased capillary permeability, which produces the redness, heat and swelling of the acute inflammatory response. Remodeling (A) is incorrect because it is the later stage of wound healing or bone repair, in which fibroblasts and osteoclasts remodel the tissue. Fever (B) is incorrect because it is caused by pyrogens (such as interleukin-1) acting on the hypothalamus. Apoptosis (D) is incorrect because it is programmed cell death, which does not involve mast cell release.

questions.text: The commonest helminthic infection is:
questions.explanation: Ascariasis (B) is correct because Ascaris lumbricoides, the large roundworm, is the commonest human helminth worldwide, infecting hundreds of millions of people, particularly children in warm areas with poor sanitation, because the eggs are very hardy and are spread by the faecal-oral route in soil, food and water. Ankylostomiasis (A) (hookworm), taeniasis (C) (tapeworm) and strongyloidiasis (D) are incorrect because, although they are common in the tropics, they are less common than ascariasis.

questions.text: Auto infection is a common phenomenon in:
questions.explanation: Enterobiasis (A) is correct because in pinworm infection (Enterobius vermicularis) the female worm lays eggs on the perianal skin at night, which causes itching; the child scratches, the eggs lodge under the fingernails and are carried back to the mouth, so the person re-infects himself or herself (autoinfection). Retroinfection, in which eggs hatch on the skin and larvae move back into the bowel, can also occur. Ankylostomiasis (B) is incorrect because hookworm larvae penetrate the skin from the soil, so infection is acquired from the environment. Schistosomiasis (C) is incorrect because the cercariae from freshwater snails penetrate the skin and the worms cannot multiply in the human host. Trichuriasis (D) is incorrect because whipworm eggs must mature in the soil for about 2 to 3 weeks before they become infective, so direct autoinfection does not occur. Treatment of pinworm is albendazole or mebendazole for the whole household, with hygiene measures.

questions.text: Maturational crises include:

options.C: Retirement from work, death of a loved one
options.D: Puberty onset, loss of a job

questions.explanation: Marriage, birth of a child (A) is correct because maturational (developmental) crises are the predictable stressful transitions that occur at stages of normal life, such as puberty, leaving home, marriage, the birth of a child, middle age and retirement, and both marriage and the birth of a child belong to this group. College graduation, divorce (B) is incorrect because divorce is a situational crisis, even though graduation is a developmental event. Retirement from work, death of a loved one (C) is incorrect because the death of a loved one is a situational (accidental) crisis, even though retirement is a developmental event. Puberty onset, loss of a job (D) is incorrect because losing a job is a situational crisis, even though puberty is a maturational event. Option A is the only choice in which both events are maturational. Situational crises are sudden, unexpected events such as job loss, divorce, death, rape or a disaster, and adventitious crises are disasters such as war, floods and violence.

questions.text: A situation where a mother denies the child to watch TV following poor grades is an example of:
questions.explanation: Negative punishment (B) is correct because in operant conditioning negative punishment means taking away a desirable stimulus (here the privilege of watching TV) after an undesired behaviour (poor grades), to reduce the chance that the behaviour will be repeated. Positive punishment (A) is incorrect because it means adding an unpleasant stimulus after the behaviour (for example extra chores or a scolding). Negative reinforcement (C) is incorrect because it means taking away an unpleasant stimulus after a desired behaviour in order to increase that behaviour (for example removing a chore when the child does well). Positive reinforcement (D) is incorrect because it means adding a pleasant stimulus after a desired behaviour to increase that behaviour (for example praise or a reward for good grades). A way to remember: positive means adding, negative means removing; reinforcement increases the behaviour, and punishment decreases it.

questions.text: In cognitive learning theory, enhanced rehearsals which serves as useful memory aids include:
questions.explanation: Retention (B) is correct because in Bandura's social cognitive (observational) learning theory the four processes are attention, retention, reproduction and motivation; retention is the process of remembering what was observed, and it is improved by mental and physical rehearsal, by coding the information into images or words, and by memory aids. Imitation (A) is incorrect because it is the outcome of observational learning (reproduction of the modelled behaviour) and not a memory process. Attention (C) is incorrect because it is the first step, in which the learner notices the model and the behaviour. Motivation (D) is incorrect because it is the reason that the learner performs the behaviour, which depends on expected reinforcement or punishment.

questions.text: A side effect of Isoniazid is:
questions.explanation: Peripheral neuropathy (B) is correct because isoniazid interferes with the metabolism of pyridoxine (vitamin B6), which causes numbness, tingling and burning of the hands and feet, and it is prevented by giving pyridoxine (vitamin B6) with isoniazid, particularly to children, pregnant women, people living with HIV and malnourished patients. Isoniazid can also cause hepatitis. Orange discoloration of urine (A) is incorrect because it is caused by rifampicin (which also colours tears and sweat). Optic neuritis (C) is incorrect because it is caused by ethambutol (red-green colour blindness and loss of visual acuity). Hyperuricemia (D) is incorrect because it is caused by pyrazinamide (which can lead to gout and joint pain).

questions.text: Protease inhibitors include:
questions.explanation: Lopinavir (D) is correct because it is a protease inhibitor (PI), usually given with ritonavir as a booster (LPV/r), and it blocks the HIV protease enzyme so that immature, non-infectious virus particles are produced. Other examples are atazanavir (ATV/r) and darunavir. Lamivudine (A) is incorrect because it is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI). Tenofovir (B) is incorrect because it is a nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NtRTI, grouped with the NRTIs). Nevirapine (C) is incorrect because it is a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI). Dolutegravir is an integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI), the class used in the first-line regimen (TLD) in Kenya.

questions.text: The antidote for warfarin is:
questions.explanation: Vitamin K (A) is correct because warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist that blocks the production of the clotting factors II, VII, IX and X in the liver, so an overdose (a high INR, bleeding) is reversed with vitamin K (phytomenadione), and in severe bleeding fresh frozen plasma or prothrombin complex concentrate is added for a faster effect. Protamine sulphate (B) is incorrect because it is the antidote for heparin. Streptokinase (C) is incorrect because it is a thrombolytic (fibrinolytic) drug that dissolves clots, and it would worsen bleeding. Tranexamic acid (D) is incorrect because it is an antifibrinolytic used to control bleeding (for example in postpartum haemorrhage and trauma), and it is not the specific antidote to warfarin. The INR is monitored in patients on warfarin (therapeutic range 2 to 3).
